questions.explanation: The inward force is m times omega squared times r, so 2.0 times 2.25 times 0.50 gives 2.25 N. Using the diameter as the radius or forgetting to square the angular speed both give wrong answers.

The reading equals the true weight because the acceleration is not produced by the contact force.
options.misconception: believes the contact force cannot change the reading

options.text: The reading falls below the true weight because the person is travelling upward through the air.
options.misconception: confuses upward motion with upward acceleration

options.text: The reading is unchanged because only gravity acts on the person inside a lifted car.
options.misconception: assumes gravity is the only force acting in the car

questions.explanation: The floor must push harder than mg to accelerate the person upward, so the reading exceeds the true weight. Constant upward velocity would leave the reading unchanged, which is what option B assumes.
questions.hint: Acceleration, not velocity, sets the reading.

questions.topic: Angular speed of a conical pendulum
questions.learningObjective: Interpret measured conical pendulum data against the standard relation
questions.stem: In the notebook I logged three pendulum trials with the bob swinging horizontally: radius 0.60 m at 30 degrees gave 3.07 rad/s, radius 0.40 m at 40 degrees gave 3.42 rad/s, and radius 0.50 m at 20 degrees gave 2.99 rad/s. Which entry is consistent with the relation omega squared equals g tan theta over r?

options.text: The 0.40 m radius trial, because the steeper string angle should always produce the largest speed.
options.misconception: assumes the largest reading must be the consistent one

options.text: The 0.60 m radius trial, because 3.07 rad/s squared is near 9.4 and g tan 30 over 0.60 is 9.44.
The 0.50 m radius trial, because a small angle with a mid radius gives a balanced and reliable result.
options.misconception: picks the trial that looks reasonable rather than the one that fits

options.text: None of the three trials, because the angular speed of a conical pendulum cannot be predicted.
options.misconception: believes the conical pendulum speed cannot be predicted

questions.explanation: For the first trial g tan 30 divided by 0.60 equals 9.44 and 3.07 squared is 9.43, so that reading matches the relation. The other two trials fail it, so their larger or smaller numbers do not make them correct.
questions.hint: Square each reading and compare with g tan theta over r.

options.misconception: confuses rotation with the absence of net torque

options.text: The angular momentum decreases steadily because the drive torque opposes the rotation.
options.misconception: ignores that the two torques cancel

options.text: The angular momentum increases because the friction torque always speeds the platform up.
options.misconception: assumes friction always adds energy to the motion

questions.explanation: For a point mass moving in a circle the angular momentum is m v r with the radius perpendicular to the velocity, giving 2 times 3 times 4 equals 24. The other options change the formula or the geometry.

questions.topic: A skater speeding up by drawing in the arms
questions.learningObjective: Explain why drawing in the arms speeds up a spinning skater
questions.stem: During the club demo of the spinning stool, I asked the audience to write down why pulling the arms inward makes the skater turn faster.

answer.exemplar: Pulling the arms inward reduces the moment of inertia about the vertical axis. With negligible external torque the angular momentum I omega is conserved, so reducing I must increase omega. The extra rotational kinetic energy is supplied by the work done by the muscles pulling the arms inward against their centrifugal resistance.

questions.explanation: A strong answer links the reduced moment of inertia to conserved angular momentum and notes that the arms do work to add kinetic energy. A weak answer merely asserts that the skater speeds up.
questions.hint: Conservation of angular momentum, not of energy.

questions.stem: Rethinking the note about the whirled weight, I wrote a short explanation of why a body on a circular path needs a force pointing to the centre.

answer.exemplar: The velocity of a body travelling in a circle changes direction continuously, so the acceleration is directed towards the centre even when the speed is constant. The speed itself may stay the same, so the force is not needed to keep the body moving but to keep it on the circle.

questions.explanation: A good answer identifies the inward force as the cause of the changing direction of the velocity, and separates it from the speed, which need not change. A poor answer says the force keeps the body moving.

questions.topic: When the angular momentum of a body is unchanged
questions.learningObjective: Explain when a spinning body keeps a constant angular momentum
questions.stem: Explaining to the beginners why a spinning platform keeps its angular momentum, I wrote a paragraph on the role of torque.

answer.exemplar: The rate of change of angular momentum of a body is equal to the net external torque acting on it, so angular momentum stays unchanged whenever the torques balance. A platform driven by a motor against friction has a drive torque and a friction torque of equal size and opposite sense, so its angular momentum remains constant even while it turns. Constant angular momentum therefore does not require zero torque, only zero net torque.

questions.explanation: A good answer states that only a net torque changes angular momentum and that balanced torques leave it unchanged, giving a worked case. A poor answer says momentum is always conserved without mentioning torque.
questions.hint: It is the net torque, not each torque, that matters.

questions.learningObjective: Write an account of how an inward force is produced on a circular path
questions.stem: Spending the hour after dusk on the whirled weight, I wrote my own account of how the inward force is produced.

answer.exemplar: On the horizontal carousel the inward force comes from the pull of the radial arms that hold the lens blank in place. That pull is always at right angles to the direction of travel, so it does no work and the speed of the blank stays constant while the direction of its velocity changes continuously. Because the velocity keeps turning, the blank follows a circle of constant radius instead of a straight line.

questions.explanation: A good answer names the source of the inward force, such as a tension or a normal reaction, and connects it to the turning of the velocity. A weak answer says the force pushes the body forwards.
questions.hint: An inward force turns the velocity without speeding it up.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Apparent weight of a person in an accelerating lift
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the scale reading while a lift slows as it descends
questions.stem: Calculating what the platform scale would show on the way down, I used a person of mass 65 kg in a lift slowing at 2.5 m/s squared as it descends. What is the reading?
questions.explanation: While the lift slows as it descends the floor pushes up with N equals m times g minus a, which is 65 times 7.31 giving 475.2 N, below the true weight. Using g plus a would wrongly give a reading above the true weight.
questions.hint: A downward acceleration means less upward push.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Banking angle needed to hold a car on a level curve
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the banking angle for a slow service road curve
questions.stem: Working through the banking of the circular apron outside the dome, I used a speed of 12 m/s on a curve of radius 80 m. What banking angle does a frictionless road need?
questions.explanation: The frictionless condition gives tan theta equals v squared over r g, which is 144 over 784.8 giving 0.1835, whose angle is 10.4 degrees. Using the diameter instead of the radius gives about 20 degrees, which is the usual mistake here.
questions.hint: tan theta equals v squared over r g.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Angular speed of a conical pendulum
questions.learningObjective: Combine angle and radius data for a conical pendulum
questions.stem: Setting up the string and bob pendulum on the balcony for the club members, I planned two measurements: the radius of the circle and the angle of the string. What follows?

options.text: The angle sets the ratio of the tension components, and the radius then fixes the tension itself.
options.misconception: assigns the radius the wrong role in the relation

options.text: The angle sets the ratio of the tension components, and the radius then fixes the angular speed.
The radius sets the ratio of the tension components, and the angle then fixes the angular speed.
options.misconception: swaps which quantity sets the component ratio

options.text: The angle and the radius together fix the tension only, and the angular speed follows from the string length.
options.misconception: thinks the angular speed depends on the string length

questions.explanation: The vertical and horizontal parts of the tension are in the ratio given by the angle, and the horizontal part must provide m omega squared r over the radius. Option C swaps the roles of the angle and the radius in that relation.
questions.hint: The angle gives the ratio, the radius gives the speed.
